cards.text: Paul, called to be an apostle, is writing to everyone in Rome who is loved by God (Romans 1:1, 7). He just spent a whole chapter on believers who don't agree about food and special days (Romans 14:2, 5). Now he turns to the ones he calls strong, and he says WE, so he's counting himself in.

cards.question: Paul says the strong ought to do what with the shortcomings of the weak?
True or false: Paul tells the strong it's fine to please themselves first.

cards.text: So if it's not about pleasing yourself, who is it about? Paul says each of us should please his neighbor, and yes, friend, that includes the one who borrowed your ladder in March and still has it.

cards.question: True or false: Paul says to please your neighbor just to keep him off your back.

cards.text: Then Paul brings out the best example there is: even Christ did not please Himself. And Paul quotes Scripture to show it (Psalm 69:9).

cards.question: In the Scripture Paul quotes, what has fallen on Christ?

cards.text: Paul says everything written in the past was written for our instruction. Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer under manuals for appliances nobody owned anymore, and THIS one is still good.

cards.question: Paul says that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have ___.

cards.text: Then Paul says, may the God who gives endurance and encouragement grant them harmony with one another in Christ Jesus. Harmony, friend, not everybody humming their own tune in a different key.

cards.question: Paul asks for harmony so the believers in Rome can do what together?

cards.text: Now Paul lands the line this whole section has been building to: accept one another. Not nod politely and switch seats, friend, ACCEPT.

cards.question: Paul says, "Accept one another, then, just as ___ accepted you."
True or false: Paul says accepting one another brings glory to God.

cards.text: Then Paul explains. Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs.

cards.question: Paul says Christ did this so that who may glorify God for His mercy?

cards.text: Then Paul backs it up with Scripture: "Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name." (Psalm 18:49) And he's not done, friend, not even CLOSE.

cards.question: Paul quotes Scripture AGAIN, and this time the Gentiles are told to rejoice. Rejoice with whom?
And AGAIN Paul quotes Scripture. True or false: this one calls only some of the peoples to praise the Lord.

cards.text: And once more, Isaiah the prophet says the Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles (Isaiah 11:10). Jesse was King David's father (Ruth 4:22).

cards.question: In Isaiah's words, what will the Gentiles do in the Root of Jesse?

cards.text: Paul ends with this: may the God of hope fill them with all joy and peace. Hope AGAIN, friend, he keeps circling back to it like I circle the oven when the timer hits ten seconds.

cards.question: Paul says God fills them with joy and peace as they do what?
True or false: Paul says they will overflow with hope by their own strength.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 2 quotes "Accept one another, then, just as ___ accepted you.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The blank is the last word of Romans 15:4, so the baker is finishing the verse's wording. The story card before it sets up 'instruction', which points toward 'wisdom' just as well as 'hope'. Nothing told so far leads the baker to 'hope', so the pick comes down to luck. Ask about meaning instead, for example what the Scriptures written in the past are for.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This card only restates Romans 15:8, with none of Papa Dorin's voice. It also gives no context for 'the circumcised', so the baker can't see the contrast that card 5 asks about. No card in the walkthrough sets up Jews and Gentiles together. Without that, 'The Gentiles' over 'The priests' or 'The angels' is close to a guess.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question says 'Christ did this', which points back to card 4. Card 4 is no longer on screen, so the question doesn't say what 'this' is.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The card quotes 'Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles...' but never says who the 'I' is. It only says 'Paul backs it up with Scripture'.

rule.text: When he quotes someone speaking as "I," he says who it is first. For example, "Then the prophet says, 'And I asked…'" (Isa 40:6).

findings.problem: In Romans 15:13, Paul says 'may the God of hope fill you'. The question turns that wish into a plain statement: 'Paul says God fills them'. It should keep Paul's 'may'. The question also uses 'them' without saying who they are.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The statement says 'they will overflow with hope' but never says who 'they' are. It leans on earlier cards that are no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: Several story cards are flat restatements with no personality: stop 1 card 6, and stop 2 cards 4 and 9. The jokes that are there (the ladder, humming in a different key, switching seats, the oven timer) are mild, nice-dad lines. None of them reach a real laugh.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
